title: Why Observability Unification Is Becoming an IT Operations Imperative
summary: New research from EMA showcases why observability unification is a high priority for IT operations teams, leading them to rethink their approach in response to tool sprawl and evolving AI goals.
body_markdown:
For years, enterprise IT teams have heard that more data would lead to better observability outcomes. In reality, today’s operations teams have more telemetry, alerts, logs, dashboards, and domain-specific tools than ever before. However, when a critical service slows or degrades, a cloud dependency fails, or users start calling the service desk, all that visibility often leaves teams ill equipped to pinpoint what is actually causing the issue.


## Tool Sprawl Has Created Inefficiencies


Network, system, application, cloud, security, and service desk teams have all evolved rapidly, each bringing their own specialized tools, metrics, and workflows. When something goes wrong, everyone may be looking at accurate information, but not necessarily the same information. The result is often a large group of IT professionals participating in a time-consuming war room without the necessary details to tell the whole story. This leaves operations teams rich in data but poor in shared context.


The impact shows up in the moments that matter most, with incident response meetings taking longer than they should. The long troubleshooting cycles, competing theories, and delayed decisions tend to focus on proving where the problem is not, debating symptoms instead of isolating causes. Service owners struggle to connect infrastructure behavior to user experience. All while IT leaders and corporate executives demand faster response and better accountability to reduce business impact. Fragmented visibility is making it difficult, if not nearly impossible, to eliminate this inefficient cycle.


## The Goal of Unifying Observability


The challenges presented by tool sprawl have ultimately led many organizations to unify their[observability](https://www.netscout.com/observability) strategy. However, the true driver may be business demands. When defining project scope, adding too many tools adds unnecessary costs and complexity, effectively creating a worse bottleneck. Fragmented workflows, inconsistent data, and a lack of trusted analysis of how infrastructure and applications connect to services the business relies on is an unsustainable model. Simultaneously, collapsing every tool into a single platform is unlikely, due to unique technical requirements.


Successful unification incorporates strategy, governance, integration expertise, and a data foundation strong enough to support both human decision-making and emerging AI-driven operations. Ultimately, the real goal of creating a shared operational context across multiple network domains will help teams better understand service health, user experience, dependencies, and business impact from a common perspective.


## Key Takeaways from the New EMA Observability Report


A new research report from Enterprise Management Associates (EMA), “[The Reality of Observability Unification in Modern IT Operations](https://www.netscout.com/reports/the-reality-of-observability-unification-in-modern-it-operations) ,” takes a closer look at these challenges and opportunities. Based on input from 356 IT tool experts involved in observability unification initiatives, the report explores what is driving these projects, where enterprises are making progress, how AI is reshaping expectations, where ServiceOps fits, and what outcomes organizations can achieve moving from fragmented monitoring environments to coordinated action.


> One finding is especially telling: Only 42 percent of respondents said they are fully confident in their observability unification strategies, with many citing the complexity of the effort as a major challenge.


For teams trying to reduce war room friction, improve collaboration, and build a stronger foundation for AI-enabled operations, this research is worth your time.
